title: The Maggid's Bootlaces
hookLine: Buber retold Hasidic tales to show God in ordinary meeting
carry: in the Hasidic tales, God is met in ordinary acts
tomorrow: what's the difference between "no" and "not yet"?

lines: TAPE IT, OR TELL THE LADLE'S STORY?
...TO WATCH HIS TEACHER TIE HIS BOOTS.
cards: Noa spent Sunday boxing up her grandfather's kitchen. Saba David is moving to a smaller place. Her mom kept saying tape it and keep going.
Saba kept stopping to tell the story of a soup ladle. Which of them was doing it right? Buber would have noticed that ladle.
He retold the tales of the Hasidim, and one answers yesterday's question. A disciple says he didn't travel to his teacher, the Maggid of Mezeritch, to learn Torah from him.
He went to watch the Maggid unlace his boots and lace them up again.

teach.h: A WHOLE PERSON IN TIED BOOTS.
teach.b: For Buber, that tale holds the heart of Hasidism. God isn't found by escaping ordinary life. A whole person shows up in how he ties his boots, and holiness happens in the meeting, in eating, working, walking, talking.
He loved another tale, from the rabbi of Kotzk. Where does God live?
Wherever we let Him in. That's view one, and it's hallow the everyday at full volume. Now the other voice, from inside the same world of study.
Gershom Scholem, a historian of Jewish mysticism, said Buber's picture was beautiful and partial. Buber leaned on the tales and set aside much of the Hasidic teaching itself.

teach.h: THE KITCHEN ISN'T OUTSIDE THE HOLY.
teach.b: And in those teachings, Scholem argued, the ordinary thing isn't the point. The point is the holy sparks hidden inside it, lifted back to God by devotion, and the self quieted until only God remains.
On Scholem's reading, Hasidism is demanding inner work, not a gentle love of the moment. Put them side by side.

teach.h: IN THE HASIDIC TALES, GOD IS MET IN ORDINARY ACTS.
teach.b: Buber guards the stories Hasidim themselves told, where boots and ladles matter. Scholem guards the harder discipline behind them. Both agree on one thing: the kitchen is not outside the holy.

how: Hasidic communities tell and retell stories of their rebbes, and the teaching of serving God through ordinary physical life is part of Hasidic thought; Buber's collections of the tales are read widely, and Scholem's critique is studied beside them.

o: fixing a strict daily schedule for prayer and study
keeping a weekday quiet so the holy day feels special
treating ordinary acts and meetings as a place to meet God

games.q: two readings of Hasidism — tap the pairs.
p: came to watch his teacher tie his boots
God lives wherever we let Him in
lift the hidden sparks to God

s: Buber retold Hasidic tales to show God met in ordinary life
for him the tied boots were the heart of it.
Scholem thought Buber's tales gave the whole picture of Hasidism
he called it partial: the Hasidic teachings stress lifting sparks and quieting the self.
in the tale, the disciple traveled to hear his teacher's Torah
he says he came to watch him unlace and lace his boots.

games.q: a classmate reads the boots tale and says: 'so Hasidism is basically mindfulness.' what's the strongest case Scholem would make back?
o: the teachings aim past the boots, at sparks lifted to God by devotion.
Hasidism has nothing to do with ordinary life; it's all about prayer.
the tales are made up, so they tell us nothing about Hasidim at all.
games.why: Scholem didn't throw out the tales; he said the Hasidic teachings point through the ordinary thing to the holy sparks within it.

practice: Choose one thing you do without thinking: pour a glass of water, wash a cup, tie a shoe. Do it now, slowly, start to finish, as though someone had traveled a long way to watch. Let your hands finish before your mind moves on.

wordCard.voice: Hallow the everyday: Buber's reading of the Hasidic tales, that God is met inside ordinary acts and meetings, not only apart from them.

orig.note: Hebrew: holiness. to hallow is to make or treat something as holy.

carryVoice: Keep this one close: in the hasidic tales, god is met in ordinary acts. Boots, ladles and moving boxes count too.

sources.ref: Martin Buber, Tales of the Hasidim: Early Masters (Rabbi Leib, son of Sarah, on watching the Maggid of Mezeritch lace his boots)
Martin Buber, The Way of Man According to the Teaching of Hasidism, closing section (the rabbi of Kotzk: God dwells wherever man lets Him in)
Gershom Scholem, 'Martin Buber's Interpretation of Hasidism' (in The Messianic Idea in Judaism)
